t: Maximum Binary Concatenation of Three Numbers
o: With only three numbers (each ≤ 127, so ≤ 7 bits), there are just 3! = 6 orders; evaluate each concatenation and take the max. Concatenating x after v is v shifted left by bitLength(x), OR x. Example 1: orders of [1,2,3] give max "11110" = 30 via [3,1,2]. Example 2 confirms the identity order can win. A greedy comparator (like 'Largest Number') also works: place a before b iff concat(a,b) > concat(b,a).
k: Only 6 permutations exist for n = 3, so brute force is trivially fast and provably correct.
Concatenation is (acc << bitLength(x)) | x with no leading zeros involved.
Alternatively, sorting by the pairwise comparator concat(a,b) > concat(b,a) yields an optimal order.

a.i: Enumerate every ordering, fold the numbers into one integer via shift-and-or, and keep the maximum. With n = 3 this is constant time and impossible to get wrong.
s: For each, fold: acc = (acc << bitLength(nums[p])) | nums[p].
a.t: O(1) — six fixed permutations of three elements

a.i: Generalizes beyond n = 3: sort so that a precedes b whenever appending b to a beats appending a to b. Exchanging any adjacent inverted pair never decreases the result, so the sorted order is optimal — the same argument as LeetCode's 'Largest Number'.
s: Sort descending by cat(a,b) vs cat(b,a).
Fold the sorted sequence with shift-and-or.
a.t: O(1) here (sorting 3 elements); O(n log n · n) in general due to comparator cost

w: Permutation brute force is the safest interview answer for n = 3; bring up the comparator only if asked to generalize. Pitfalls: computing bit length wrong for powers of two (use 32 − clz, not floor(log2)), and JavaScript's bitwise ops being 32-bit (fine here since the result ≤ 21 bits, but multiply-shift keeps it explicit). Edge cases: duplicate values, value 1 (single bit). Follow-up: generalize to n up to 1e5 (comparator sort with big-number comparison).
